items.title: Advaith Homes
items.shortDescription: A buyer-side property guidance platform: a deep content library and five financial calculators, all client-editable.
items.description: A WordPress platform for a UK property consultancy that supports buyers rather than listing houses. The site organises a large body of guidance around the stages of a purchase, puts five financial calculators in front of the questions people actually get stuck on, and routes anyone who needs a professional to the right one.
highlights: Five financial calculators: total cost to buy, stamp duty, first-time-buyer savings plan, affordability and budget
Guidance library structured by purchase stage rather than by page
Ask an Expert routing to surveyors, solicitors and mortgage advisers
Custom WordPress theme — every section editable by the client

caseStudy._note: Written from the live site. The Brief and Outcome describe what is observably there — replace them with the real engagement story, and fill in role and duration, before this goes public.
caseStudy.brief: A UK property consultancy that works for the buyer rather than the seller. They needed a site that could carry a large and growing body of guidance, host the financial tools their clients kept asking for, and connect people to vetted professionals — all of it editable by the team without a developer.
caseStudy.challenge: Buying a home in the UK is a process most people go through two or three times in a lifetime, against professionals who do it daily. The information exists but is scattered, and the numbers that decide whether a purchase is possible — stamp duty, the true total cost, what is actually affordable — are exactly the ones buyers get wrong. A conventional estate-agency site, built around listings, answers none of that.
caseStudy.approach: The content architecture follows the purchase itself rather than a page hierarchy: buying a home, property knowledge, tools, professionals. Five calculators sit at the points where buyers stall — total cost to buy, stamp duty, a first-time-buyer savings plan, affordability and budget — so the guidance and the arithmetic live in the same place. Everything runs on a custom WordPress theme with structured content types, so new guides and updated rates are a content edit rather than a release. Coverage spans England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, which the tools account for.
caseStudy.outcome: A property platform that gives buyers the guidance and the numbers in one place, and gives the consultancy a site their own team maintains — with the Ask an Expert route turning readers into enquiries.

items.title: The Cane House
items.shortDescription: Freshly pressed sugarcane juice — online ordering and event catering, currently in build.
items.description: An online ordering and event catering site for a UK sugarcane juice brand. The holding page is live while the storefront is built: flavour ordering, and enquiry-to-booking for event catering.
highlights: Holding page live now — “Pressed Fresh. Served Cool.”
Event catering enquiry and booking flow

caseStudy._note: This project is still in build. The Outcome is deliberately empty — nothing to report until it ships. Replace the narrative with the real engagement story before publishing.
caseStudy.brief: A UK brand pressing sugarcane juice to order wanted to sell online and take event catering bookings, rather than relying on being found in person.
caseStudy.challenge: The product is made fresh and served cold, which makes it a poor fit for conventional shipping-based e-commerce. Ordering has to work around collection and events instead of a courier, and the catering side is an enquiry with a date and a headcount rather than an item in a basket.
caseStudy.approach: A holding page went up first so the brand had a working address while the storefront was built. Ordering is being modelled around flavours and collection rather than shipping, with event catering handled as a dated enquiry flow instead of a checkout — two different jobs that a single generic cart would do badly.

items.title: Interior Design Studio
items.shortDescription: A portfolio-led studio website where the work does the selling.
items.description: A restrained, image-first website for an interior design practice. Projects are the primary navigation, each with a full case layout, and the enquiry flow is available from every scroll position without ever interrupting the browsing experience.

caseStudy.brief: A design practice whose work sold itself in person but not online. The old site buried projects three clicks deep behind a services menu.
caseStudy.challenge: Photography was the product, but the previous template compressed every image into a 400px card and put a stock hero above them. Enquiries came almost entirely from Instagram, not the website.
caseStudy.approach: Projects became the primary navigation rather than a sub-page. Each one got a full case layout with responsive image sources at four widths, and the enquiry route was made available from any scroll position without a pop-up.
caseStudy.outcome: A site the studio sends people to instead of a portfolio PDF, with the work at the size it deserves.

items.title: Artisan Goods Store
items.shortDescription: A small-catalogue store built around variants and fast checkout.
items.description: An online store for a handmade goods brand with a modest catalogue but complex variants. Product pages handle size, finish and personalisation without turning into a form, and checkout is reduced to the fewest steps the payment flow allows.

caseStudy.brief: A maker brand selling roughly forty products, each with size, finish and personalisation options.
caseStudy.challenge: Variants multiplied into hundreds of combinations. On the previous platform every option was a separate dropdown, so the product page read as a tax form and abandonment was concentrated there.
caseStudy.approach: Options were modelled as a single variant matrix with live availability and price, so choosing a size greys out the finishes that don't exist. Checkout was cut to two steps and order and stock sync run over webhooks.
caseStudy.outcome: A product page that answers the question 'can I actually buy this one' before the customer has to guess.

items.title: Operations Dashboard
items.shortDescription: An internal tool that replaced a shared spreadsheet.
items.description: A browser-based operations dashboard for a logistics team: job records, status workflow, role-based access and exportable reporting. Built to be usable on a phone in the field and on a desktop in the office, with validation that prevents the data mess the spreadsheet allowed.

caseStudy.brief: A logistics team running daily operations out of one shared spreadsheet that four people edited at once.
caseStudy.challenge: No validation, no history, and no way to see who changed what. Jobs were lost to overwritten rows, and the field crew couldn't use it on a phone at all.
caseStudy.approach: A browser-based tool with a real data model, role-based permissions and a workflow state per job. Built mobile-first because most edits happen from a van, with CSV and print output so the office reporting habit survived the migration.
caseStudy.outcome: Job records that can't be silently overwritten, and a field crew that stopped phoning the office to ask about status.

items.title: Property Listings Portal
items.shortDescription: Search, filter and enquire — without a page reload.
items.description: A property portal with map and list views, multi-criteria filtering, saved searches and per-listing enquiry routing. Listings are managed through a custom admin area so the agency's team can publish without developer involvement.

caseStudy.brief: An agency whose listings were re-typed by hand into a website, a portal feed and a printed sheet.
caseStudy.challenge: Listings went stale within days, and buyers filtering by more than one criterion triggered a full page reload each time.
caseStudy.approach: One admin area as the source of truth, with client-side filtering across every criterion so refining a search is instant. Map and list views share the same result set rather than being separate pages.
caseStudy.outcome: Agents publish once, and buyers can narrow twelve criteria without ever waiting for a page load.

items.title: Clinic Booking Website
items.shortDescription: Appointments booked directly, without a phone call.
items.description: A multi-practitioner clinic website with service information, practitioner profiles and an appointment request flow tied to real availability. Accessibility was a first-class requirement given the patient demographic.

caseStudy.brief: A multi-practitioner clinic taking every appointment by phone during opening hours only.
caseStudy.challenge: Reception spent mornings on the phone, and patients who needed an evening appointment had no way to ask for one. A significant share of patients use screen readers or large text.
caseStudy.approach: Accessibility was a build requirement, not a review step: full keyboard operation, real labels, and contrast checked against WCAG AA throughout. Requests are tied to actual practitioner availability so the clinic never has to decline a slot it already offered.
caseStudy.outcome: Appointment requests arriving outside opening hours, and a booking flow that works with a screen reader end to end.

items.title: SaaS Product Launch Page
items.shortDescription: One page, one action, measured end to end.
items.description: A launch page for a software product: a tight narrative from problem to proof to sign-up, with a single conversion goal, event tracking on every meaningful interaction and a structure ready for A/B variants.

caseStudy.brief: A software team with a launch date and no page to send traffic to.
caseStudy.challenge: Paid traffic was scheduled before the page existed, and the team needed to know which section of the argument was losing people.
caseStudy.approach: A single-goal page structured as problem, proof, sign-up, with analytics events on each meaningful interaction and a component structure that lets any section be swapped for an A/B variant without a rebuild.
caseStudy.outcome: A page that shipped ahead of the campaign and can be reasoned about with data rather than opinion.

items.title: Editorial CMS Website
items.shortDescription: A content model editors don't need training to use.
items.description: A publishing website with custom content types, editorial workflow, scheduled publishing and structured article components. Editors compose from reusable blocks, so layouts stay consistent no matter who publishes.

items.title: Manufacturing Company Website
items.shortDescription: A technical catalogue made navigable for buyers.
items.description: A corporate website for a manufacturer with a large product catalogue, specification tables, downloadable datasheets and a quote request flow. The challenge was making dense technical information findable rather than impressive.

items.title: Student Portal
items.shortDescription: One login for admissions, materials and results.
items.description: A student-facing portal covering admission applications, course materials, schedules and results, with separate staff and administrator views. Sessions, permissions and document access were designed around institutional policy from the start.

items.title: Restaurant Website Redesign
items.shortDescription: A rebuild that made the menu the point again.
items.description: A redesign for a restaurant group whose previous site buried the menu behind a slideshow. The rebuild put menus, hours, location and reservations within one tap of the landing screen and cut the page weight substantially.

items.title: Conference Registration Page
items.shortDescription: Schedule, speakers and registration in one scroll.
items.description: A single-page site for a professional conference: agenda, speaker profiles, venue details and tiered ticket registration, built to hold up under a concentrated traffic spike on announcement day.

items.title: Non-Profit Programme Site
items.description: A website for a non-profit covering programmes, impact reports, volunteer sign-up and recurring donations. Every content area is editable by the organisation's own team, because their update frequency made anything else impractical.
